text: DSH Plugin Dependency Graph 是一个面向 DSH Web 客户端的插件依赖关系查看器。它在设置界面加入只读图表，并由服务端路由提供当前运行时的图数据，也可在独立页面查看。用户可以观察插件提供和注入的服务、查找插件或服务名称、筛选节点并查看选中节点的依赖详情，还能分别查看主机与浏览器运行时的关系。适合排查 DSH 插件组合和理解服务由谁提供、被谁使用；代码未声明额外密钥或外部服务。

DSH Plugin Dependency Graph adds a read-only graph to DSH web settings and a standalone viewer. Inspect plugin service dependencies, search plugin or service names, and review selected nodes. Host and browser graphs are separate. No API key or external service is declared in the inspected code.
想弄清楚 DSH 里某个服务是由哪个插件提供、又被哪些插件依赖。
DSH 插件之间的依赖关系有没有图形界面可以查看？
How can I search a DSH runtime graph for the plugins that provide or use a service?
DSH Plugin Dependency Graph 的功能「运行时依赖图」：在设置面板或独立查看页展示运行中的插件节点及服务依赖关系，帮助查看插件之间的提供与注入关系。
DSH Plugin Dependency Graph 的功能「按名称搜索依赖」：在图面板输入插件名、Loader entry ID 或提供的服务名，显示匹配节点及相关服务角色。
dsh-plugin-dependency-graph README · Introduction：English | [中文](README.zh.md)

dsh-plugin-dependency-graph README · Plugin graph：Which plugin provides the services every other plugin injects — read from the live Cordis
runtime, not from a manifest.

A settings section draws the graph, and a standalone page shows the same graph at full width.
Both render the *same* panel: the two hosts differ only in what they can supply (a locale
service, a theme, a window instead of a settings column).

dsh-plugin-dependency-graph README · Screenshots：The section, as it opens: the counts, the **status row** (a dot per state the graph has, its
count, and a click that filters to it), the drawing, and the **four-line key** in the corner.
The controls above the drawing are `← →` (selection history), zoom, reset and fullscreen.

Fullscreen. The canvas IS the fullscreen element, so everything the panel put beside it is off
screen — which is why the toolbar moves to the top line inside the canvas and the search box
takes the second.

dsh-plugin-dependency-graph README · Screenshots：A selected node. Its own description appears under the name, **Listens to** says which events it
subscribes to, and the wires split by direction — **the key in the corner names which colour is
which** — dashed where the dependency is only acquired at runtime.

dsh-plugin-dependency-graph README · Screenshots：Searching. The query is matched against package names, Loader entry ids and the services a plugin
PROVIDES, so `ctx.locale` finds whoever offers it. The matches are listed as a card, each row
carrying the package and its state — plus the service that matched, under the name, when that is
how the row was found. The drawing dims everything else. The `×` in the field clears the query and
hands the caret back.

dsh-plugin-dependency-graph README · Screenshots：The standalone viewer, opened in a new tab: the same graph at the width of a whole window. Here it
has the **`(harness)`** node selected — the runtime's own row, which carries everything no plugin
claims: the services the root fiber provides, the services it injects, and the events it listens
to. It depends on nothing, so it has incoming wires only.

dsh-plugin-dependency-graph README · The two trees：There are two Cordis runtimes, and they get two graphs:

| | Host | Browser |
|---|---|---|
| Where it runs | the Node process | the page |
| Collected by | `collectGraph(ctx)` on the host | `collectGraph(ctx.root)` in the page |
| Shown by | this section, fetched over HTTP | reported by the page, read back by the viewer |

dsh-plugin-dependency-graph README · The two trees：**They are never merged.** They are different runtimes with different plugins and different
service names, so a merged graph would not be a bigger one — it would be a wrong one. The
Browser tab is a second *source*, not a second set of nodes.

dsh-plugin-dependency-graph README · The two trees：The browser tree cannot be collected by the Node half, so the page is the only thing that can
describe it: the section POSTs what it collected to `/dsh-plugin-dependency-graph/client`, and the viewer
GETs it back (one path, two methods). The report carries **the instant it was taken**, and the
viewer prints it — a graph a reader believes is current but is not is worse than one that admits
its age.

dsh-plugin-dependency-graph README · The two trees：The browser tree's **descriptions** come from a route of their own
(`/dsh-plugin-dependency-graph/descriptions`), because the page cannot read `node_modules` while the packages
it is describing are the same ones: this half reads them and serves a name → description table.
That read is the one place the two halves differ in capability, and it is why the merge lives in
`src/describe.ts` — pure, so both halves run one implementation, while only the Node half touches
`node:fs`. Resolution tries the plugin's own tree first, then bases learned from the host's
`profileContext.dir`: measured, the obvious bases all land on the checkout, where none of the
third-party plugins are installed.

dsh-plugin-dependency-graph README · How a dependency is acquired：A plugin can take a service two ways, and the difference is not cosmetic:

- **Declared** on the plugin (`export const inject = [...]`, an `inject:` option, or the
  `@Inject` decorator) — the fiber stays pending until every one of them resolves. The plugin
  does not load without them.
- **At runtime**, through the `ctx.inject(deps, callback)` helper — the callback runs once they
  appear. The plugin loads either way; only that contribution waits.

dsh-plugin-dependency-graph README · How a dependency is acquired：Both are real dependencies, both get edges, and the second is what the `optional` mark means. A
missing *required* service is a broken composition; a missing *optional* one is the ordinary
case the callback form exists for.

dsh-plugin-dependency-graph README · How a dependency is acquired：The collection reads three things, and the distinction matters: the **Loader entries** give the
ids and package names, the **reflection store** is the authoritative provider table (keyed by
isolation symbol — the fiber's own `store` is the wrong source and would name consumers as
providers), and the **registry** supplies every live fiber, including ones started at runtime.

dsh-plugin-dependency-graph README · Reading the graph：- **The layout is data, not physics.** A node sits closer to the middle the more plugins depend on
  it, and the angle is a golden-angle walk over the ids — so the same composition draws the same
  picture on every visit, and a refresh never makes the reader find their bearings again. Hubs are
  the centre; the rim is what nothing depends on.
- **Plugins with no edges at all are COLLAPSED by default**, behind one control that says how many
  (`61 with no dependencies`). In the composition this was built against that is 31% of the picture —
  nodes with no relation to draw, holding the rim and therefore the zoom — so they are hidden rather
  than dropped: pressing the control brings them back, because "this plugin takes part in nothing" is
  itself an answer a reader comes here for. A node the search or the status filter singles out is
  drawn even when it has no edges, so following a result row always lands somewhere.
- **Refresh** re-reads the graph. It keeps whatever is on screen while it does, rather than
  blanking to a spinner: the canvas can be the fullscreen element, and an element that leaves the
  document takes fullsc
dsh-plugin-dependency-graph README · What a node reports：Selecting a node fills the detail card with everything the runtime knows about that plugin:

dsh-plugin-dependency-graph README · What a node reports：- **The package's own description**, read from its `package.json`. Absent rather than empty when
  the package does not say, or when nothing could read it — drawing no line is the truthful
  rendering of "this package does not describe itself".
- **Declared injections** — the services this entry's own patch row asks for, when it asks for any.
  Read from the ENTRY rather than from the running fiber, which is why it sits beside **Injects**
  instead of inside it: the two differ exactly when a declaration went unmet, and an entry that
  never loaded has no runtime injections at all. Absent rather than empty: 3 entries of a 194-entry
  composition declare anything, so a permanent "declares nothing" row would be a line about the
  other 191. The rest of the entry's registration — mount path, group, `isolate`, `intercept`,
  `config` — is still collected and served by the JSON route; it simply earned no rows.
- **Disabled** — a badge beside the state, on the entries that are switched off, and the state's
  missing half: a disabled entry reads `not loaded`, exactly like one that is merely waiting, and in
  that same composition all

dsh-plugin-dependency-graph README · What a node reports：**`(harness)`** is the one node that is not a plugin: it is the runtime's own row. Services
provided by a fiber with no Loader entry behind it — the root fiber, and anything started outside
the entry tree — are credited here rather than dropped, and their injections and listeners come
with them. It is what keeps `loader` and the environment rows from reading as unresolved
dependencies of everything that injects them.

dsh-plugin-dependency-graph README · What the graph reports：Two blocks sit under the drawing, and both are about work rather than about drawing:

- **Unresolved dependencies** — required services with no provider anywhere in this composition.
  Only *required* ones: an optional injection with no provider has simply not been offered yet,
  and the plugin is working as designed.
- **Isolated services** — one service name with more than one live implementation, i.e. provided
  under more than one isolation label.

dsh-plugin-dependency-graph README · The standalone viewer：A page the Node half serves as a whole document. It has no Cordis of its own, so it can only
show the host's tree plus the browser report the app sent — and it reads two things from the URL
it was opened with, because it cannot read them any other way:

dsh-plugin-dependency-graph README · The standalone viewer：| Parameter | Why |
|---|---|
| `?scheme=dark\|light` | the page styles itself with the app's `--dsw-*` tokens; the attribute that switches them is the app's, not this page's |
| `?lang=zh\|en\|ja\|ko\|es\|fr\|de` | so the new tab opens in the language the app is **in**, instead of guessing from the browser |

dsh-plugin-dependency-graph README · The standalone viewer：The locale is whitelisted against the dictionaries before it reaches the document — a query
string is not a place to trust, and that value ends up in the page's `lang` attribute. A page
opened directly (no parameter) falls back to the browser's own preferences, then to English.

The browser report lives in memory only, never on disk: it describes a runtime that exists while
the page is open, and a report that outlived a host restart would be describing something that
is not there.

dsh-plugin-dependency-graph README · Language：Seven dictionaries in `src/client/locales.ts`: `zh` and `en` (the two the shell carries) plus
`ja`, `ko`, `es`, `fr` and `de`, contributed one namespace at a time through the single-locale
overload — the language pack a profile carries owns the *definition* that makes a language
selectable, and this plugin adds only its own strings to it. It deliberately does not call
`addLanguage`.

dsh-plugin-dependency-graph README · Language：Every dictionary is typed `Record<MessagesKey, string>`, so a key added to `MessagesKey` fails to
compile until all seven carry it. Wording follows `session-messages`, which shipped these five
first: the plugins sit in one interface, so a reader must meet the same terms in both.

dsh-plugin-dependency-graph README · Layout：```text
dsh-plugin-dependency-graph-plugin/
  package.json        dsh.bundle + dsh.client declarations, exports map (private, not published)
  cordis.patch.yml    layer patch: the Loader row
  build.mjs           build script: bundles both halves, and copies the theme at build time

dsh-plugin-dependency-graph README · Layout：Routes, all under `/dsh-plugin-dependency-graph`: the graph itself, `/view` (the page), `/viewer.js`,
and `/theme.css` — plus `/client`, which takes a POST from the app and answers a GET for the viewer,
`/descriptions`, which serves the name → description table for the browser tree, and `/config`, which
takes an entry id and serves THAT entry's composed configuration.

dsh-plugin-dependency-graph README · Development：```sh
npm run build     # bundles lib/index.js, lib/client.js and lib/viewer.js
npx tsc -p tsconfig.json   # type check
```

Install as a plugin in a DSH checkout by adding this directory's `cordis.patch.yml` to the
bundle: it inserts the single Loader row. Nothing here needs the host's source to be modified —
that is a constraint this plugin is built to, not a coincidence.
